params.body:
`protection` answered 403 on 20 of the 24 measured projects, across all six owners:

```
protection: GitHub answered 403 for the protection of abovebeyond-ai/vera:
Resource not accessible by integration
```

The cause is not the App's rights but the token's. `ReadToken` downscopes at mint time to
`contents`, `metadata`, `actions`, `pull_requests`. Branch protection sits behind
`administration`, which the token never asked for. Granting the App that right was
necessary and not sufficient: a downscoped token cannot exceed the installation, but it
also never reaches it.

GitHub has no narrower right for branch protection, so the whole bundle comes along:
collaborators and teams, the webhook list, the public half of deploy keys, runner and
Actions settings. All read-only.

**The weighing**, written into the comment so the next cleanup round does not undo it:
this same token already carries `contents`, so a leak hands over the source of the whole
fleet. A repository's configuration is small next to that. One item is worth naming
anyway: a Forge deploy hook keeps its secret in the URL, so the hook list exposes a
deploy trigger. Those URLs are worth rotating on their own schedule; they were exposed to
every repo admin before this change.

The cost of leaving it: twenty projects silently blind on one dimension of maturity,
printed as `not measured` in every brief, which reads as a fault rather than as a choice.

**Test.** The existing loop walks `ReadPermissions`, so a new entry passes it unnoticed. A
second loop pins the line that does not move: every right is `read`. Verified by mutation
(`administration: write` fails with `a read token carries read rights only`).

After merge the gateway needs a tag and `rehearse.sh upgrade`; the cached read tokens on
the box live an hour, so the fleet clears on the next round or sooner if they are removed.
params.title: A read token may see a repository's configuration
